concepts.name: Reading a chain
concepts.description: Follow the path between two letters: one direction all along gives a definite relation, strict if any sign is strict.

concepts.name: Joining statements
concepts.description: Several statements that share letters merge into one chain through those letters.

concepts.name: Either–or conclusions
concepts.description: Two conclusions on the same pair, neither true alone, of which exactly one must hold.

concepts.name: Coded inequalities
concepts.description: Symbols such as @, # and $ stand for the five signs; decode them before solving.

concepts.name: The missing sign
concepts.description: Find the one sign that makes the required conclusions definitely true.

formulas.title: The path rule
formulas.prompt: When does a chain give a definite relation between two letters?
formulas.formula:
Every sign on the path points the same way (= can be ignored)
Any strict sign (> or <) ⇒ the result is strict
One sign pointing back ⇒ no definite relation
formulas.explanation: Values only rise (or only fall) along a path that never turns; if it turns, the ends can compare either way.
formulas.example: P > Q ≥ R = S ⇒ P > S. A ≥ B > C ≤ D ⇒ nothing between A and D.
formulas.commonMistake: Taking P ≥ Q ≥ R as P > R: with no strict sign the answer is only P ≥ R.
formulas.applicationPrompt: K ≤ L = M < N. What is the relation between K and N?

formulas.title: Joining statements
formulas.prompt: Two statements share a letter. How do you combine them?
formulas.formula:
Rewrite them as one chain through the shared letter
Flip a statement when needed: A ≥ B is B ≤ A
Then use the path rule
formulas.explanation: The shared letter is the only bridge between the two statements.
formulas.example: A < B ≤ C and D ≥ C ⇒ A < B ≤ C ≤ D ⇒ A < D.
formulas.commonMistake: Flipping the letters but not the sign.
formulas.applicationPrompt: P > Q and R ≥ Q. What is the relation between P and R?

formulas.title: Either–or
formulas.prompt: When is the answer "Either conclusion I or II is true"?
formulas.formula:
Neither is true alone, both are about the same two letters, and
they split the derived relation (≥ into > and =), or
they are exact opposites (> and ≤, < and ≥)
formulas.explanation: In each case exactly one of the two must hold, whatever the actual values.
formulas.example: R ≥ T: I. R > T II. R = T ⇒ either. E > F ≤ H: I. E > H II. E ≤ H ⇒ either.
formulas.commonMistake: Choosing either-or when one conclusion is already true.
formulas.applicationPrompt: A ≥ B. I. A > B. II. A = B. What is the answer?

formulas.title: Decoding the symbols
formulas.prompt: How do the usual coded phrases translate?
formulas.formula:
neither smaller than nor equal to ⇒ >
not smaller than ⇒ ≥
neither smaller nor greater ⇒ =
not greater than ⇒ ≤
neither greater than nor equal to ⇒ <
formulas.explanation: "Not smaller" leaves "greater or equal"; "neither smaller nor equal" leaves only "greater".
formulas.example: "P @ Q means P is not smaller than Q" ⇒ @ is ≥.
formulas.applicationPrompt: "P % Q means P is not greater than Q." Which sign is %?

formulas.title: The missing sign
formulas.prompt: A chain has a "?" and some conclusions must be true. How do you find the sign?
formulas.formula:
Start with a conclusion that links the two letters next to "?"
An "=" conclusion needs "=" all along its path
A strict conclusion needs at least one strict sign
Check the choice against every conclusion
formulas.explanation: The conclusion closest to the gap usually decides the sign; the others confirm it.
formulas.example: A < B ? C ≤ D with B < C required ⇒ ? is <.
formulas.commonMistake: Choosing ≥ or ≤ when a strict conclusion is required.
formulas.applicationPrompt: P = Q ? R with Q = R required. Which sign?

formulas.title: Exactly what the chain says
formulas.prompt: A chain gives P ≥ Q. Which conclusions are true: P ≥ Q, P > Q, P = Q?
formulas.formula:
Only the derived relation itself is true:
P ≥ Q gives P ≥ Q, not P > Q, not P = Q
formulas.explanation: P > Q and P = Q are each only one part of P ≥ Q.
formulas.example: M < N = O ≤ P: N ≤ P is true, P > N is not.
formulas.commonMistake: Reading a weak sign (≥) as strict.
formulas.applicationPrompt: X = Y ≤ Z. Is Z > X definitely true?

formulas.title: Skip the equals
formulas.prompt: How do "=" signs affect a path?
formulas.formula:
Ignore every = on the path;
read the direction from the other signs
formulas.explanation: An equals sign never turns the path and never makes it strict.
formulas.example: P = Q > R = S < T: P to S reads just ">" ⇒ P > S.
formulas.commonMistake: Treating = as if it weakened a strict result.
formulas.applicationPrompt: A = B = C < D. What is A compared with D?

formulas.title: Read a conclusion from the other end
formulas.prompt: A conclusion is written "T < Q" but your chain runs from Q to T. What do you do?
formulas.formula:
X < Y is the same as Y > X
X ≤ Y is the same as Y ≥ X
formulas.explanation: Swapping the letters flips the sign; the meaning is unchanged.
formulas.example: Chain gives Q > T; the conclusion T < Q is true.
formulas.commonMistake: Rejecting a true conclusion because it is written right to left.
formulas.applicationPrompt: The chain gives L ≥ J. Is "J ≤ L" true?

levels.title: Chains and Paths
levels.description: The path rule, and when either–or applies.

blocks.title: A chain is a path
blocks.body: Read P ≥ Q > R = S as a path from P to S. If every sign points the same way, the ends have a definite relation, and it is strict if any one sign is strict: P > S. If any sign points back the other way, as in A ≥ B > C ≤ D, the two ends could compare either way, and nothing definite follows.

blocks.title: The path rule
blocks.body:
All one way ⇒ definite (strict if any sign is strict)
One sign the other way ⇒ no relation
blocks.caption: "=" signs can be ignored: they never turn the path.

blocks.title: Either–or
blocks.body: Sometimes neither conclusion is true alone, but one of the two must be. R ≥ T means "R > T or R = T", so the pair I. R > T, II. R = T gives "either I or II". So does a pair of exact opposites, like E > H and E ≤ H, when nothing definite links E and H.

blocks.title: Joining two statements
blocks.body: A < B ≤ C and D ≥ C > E share the letter C. Rewrite D ≥ C as C ≤ D and join: A < B ≤ C ≤ D. Now A < D follows, but B and E meet only through B ≤ C > E, which turns, so nothing follows between them.

Answer exactly what the chain says. From M < N = O ≤ P you get N ≤ P, which does not make P > N true. Questions here never ask whether "P ≥ Q" follows from "P > Q", because answer keys differ on that.

questions.question: Which of the conclusions is definitely true?
questions.context:
Statement: P > Q ≥ R = S
Conclusions:
I. P > S
II. Q ≥ S

options.text: Only conclusion I is true
Only conclusion II is true
Either conclusion I or II is true
Neither conclusion I nor II is true
Both conclusions I and II are true

questions.explanation: I: P > Q ≥ R = S. Every sign points the same way and one is strict, so P > S: true. II: Q ≥ R = S gives Q ≥ S: true. Both are true.
solutionSteps: Find the path between the two letters of each conclusion.
I: >, ≥, = all point one way, with a strict > ⇒ P > S.
questions.method: Same direction all along the path; strict if any sign is strict.

hints.text: Follow the chain from the first letter of the conclusion to the second.
If a sign on that path points the other way (> against <, or ≥ against ≤), there is no definite relation.

commonMistakes: Thinking ≥ on the path stops P > S: one strict sign is enough.

questions.question: Which of the conclusions is definitely true?
questions.context:
Statement: A ≥ B > C ≤ D
Conclusions:
I. A > C
II. D > B

options.text: Only conclusion I is true
Only conclusion II is true
Either conclusion I or II is true
Neither conclusion I nor II is true
Both conclusions I and II are true

questions.explanation: I: A ≥ B > C, so A > C: true. II: from B to D the path is B > C ≤ D; the signs point opposite ways, so B and D have no definite relation and D > B is not true. Only I.
solutionSteps: Find the path between the two letters of each conclusion.
I: ≥ then > ⇒ A > C.
II: > then ≤ point opposite ways ⇒ no relation between B and D.
questions.method: Opposite signs on the path break the chain.

hints.text: Follow the chain from the first letter of the conclusion to the second.
If a sign on that path points the other way (> against <, or ≥ against ≤), there is no definite relation.

commonMistakes: Reading D > B from "C ≤ D" and "B > C" as if both were about D.

questions.question: Which of the conclusions is definitely true?
questions.context:
Statement: M < N = O ≤ P
Conclusions:
I. M < P
II. P > N

options.text: Only conclusion I is true
Only conclusion II is true
Either conclusion I or II is true
Neither conclusion I nor II is true
Both conclusions I and II are true

questions.explanation: I: M < N = O ≤ P, so M < P: true. II: N = O ≤ P gives N ≤ P, that is P ≥ N. P could equal N, so P > N is not certain. Only I.
solutionSteps: Find the path between the two letters of each conclusion.
I: <, =, ≤ point one way with a strict < ⇒ M < P.
II: =, ≤ ⇒ N ≤ P; with no strict sign, P > N is not certain.
questions.method: No strict sign on the path ⇒ only ≥ or ≤ can follow.

hints.text: Follow the chain from the first letter of the conclusion to the second.
If a sign on that path points the other way (> against <, or ≥ against ≤), there is no definite relation.

commonMistakes: Taking P > N because P is "after" N in the chain.

questions.question: Which of the conclusions is definitely true?
questions.context:
Statement: J ≤ K < L ≥ M > N
Conclusions:
I. K < N
II. L > N

options.text: Only conclusion I is true
Only conclusion II is true
Either conclusion I or II is true
Neither conclusion I nor II is true
Both conclusions I and II are true

questions.explanation: I: K < L ≥ M: the signs point opposite ways, so K and N have no definite relation; I is not true. II: L ≥ M > N gives L > N: true. Only II.
solutionSteps: Find the path between the two letters of each conclusion.
I: from K: <, then ≥ (opposite way) ⇒ no relation.
II: from L: ≥, > ⇒ L > N.
questions.method: Check each path for a sign that points back.

hints.text: Follow the chain from the first letter of the conclusion to the second.
If a sign on that path points the other way (> against <, or ≥ against ≤), there is no definite relation.

commonMistakes: Ignoring the ≥ between L and M and concluding K < N.

questions.question: Which of the conclusions is definitely true?
questions.context:
Statement: R ≥ S = T ≤ U
Conclusions:
I. R > T
II. R = T

options.text: Only conclusion I is true
Only conclusion II is true
Either conclusion I or II is true
Neither conclusion I nor II is true
Both conclusions I and II are true

questions.explanation: R ≥ S = T gives R ≥ T. That allows R > T or R = T, so neither I nor II is certain. But they are about the same two letters and together make up R ≥ T: exactly one of them must hold. Either I or II is true.
solutionSteps: Find the path between the two letters of each conclusion.
R ≥ S = T ⇒ R ≥ T.
Neither R > T nor R = T is certain alone.
Together they cover R ≥ T ⇒ either I or II.
questions.method: Derived ≥ split into > and = is the classic either-or.

hints.text: Find the relation between R and T first.
R ≥ T means "R > T or R = T". Are I and II those two parts?

commonMistakes: Answering "Neither" after finding that neither is certain alone.

questions.question: Which of the conclusions is definitely true?
questions.context:
Statement: E > F ≤ G < H
Conclusions:
I. E > H
II. E ≤ H

options.text: Only conclusion I is true
Only conclusion II is true
Either conclusion I or II is true
Neither conclusion I nor II is true
Both conclusions I and II are true

questions.explanation: From E to H the path is E > F ≤ G < H: the first two signs point opposite ways, so E and H have no definite relation. Neither conclusion is certain. But E > H and E ≤ H are exact opposites (between them they cover every case), so exactly one is true: either I or II.
solutionSteps: Find the path between the two letters of each conclusion.
E > F ≤ … ⇒ no relation between E and H.
E > H and E ≤ H are opposites: one must be true.
questions.method: Opposite conclusions on the same pair (> and ≤, < and ≥) give either-or when neither follows.

hints.text: Is there any definite relation between E and H?
Can E > H and E ≤ H both be false?

commonMistakes: Answering "Neither" without noticing the pair are exact opposites.

questions.question: Which of the conclusions is definitely true?
questions.context:
Statement: V ≤ W ≥ X = Y
Conclusions:
I. V < X
II. V ≥ X

options.text: Only conclusion I is true
Only conclusion II is true
Either conclusion I or II is true
Neither conclusion I nor II is true
Both conclusions I and II are true

questions.explanation: V ≤ W ≥ X: the signs point opposite ways, so V and X have no definite relation. V < X and V ≥ X are exact opposites, so one of them must be true: either I or II.
solutionSteps: Find the path between the two letters of each conclusion.
V ≤ W ≥ X ⇒ no relation between V and X.
V < X and V ≥ X cover every case between them.
questions.method: Opposites on the same pair ⇒ either-or when neither follows.

hints.text: Look at the signs between V and X.
Rewrite II as "not V < X". What does that tell you?

commonMistakes: Thinking either-or needs a derived ≥ or ≤.

questions.question: Which of the conclusions is definitely true?
questions.context:
Statement: A > B ≥ C = D
Conclusions:
I. A > D
II. A = D

options.text: Only conclusion I is true
Only conclusion II is true
Either conclusion I or II is true
Neither conclusion I nor II is true
Both conclusions I and II are true

questions.explanation: A > B ≥ C = D gives A > D: I is true. Then A = D is false, so this is not an either-or case: only I.
solutionSteps: Find the path between the two letters of each conclusion.
>, ≥, = with a strict > ⇒ A > D.
II contradicts I.
questions.method: Look for a definite conclusion before thinking about either-or.

hints.text: Follow the chain from the first letter of the conclusion to the second.
If a sign on that path points the other way (> against <, or ≥ against ≤), there is no definite relation.

commonMistakes: Answering "Either" because I and II are about the same pair.

questions.question: Which of the conclusions is definitely true?
questions.context:
Statements: P ≥ Q > R; R ≥ S = T
Conclusions:
I. P > T
II. T < Q

options.text: Only conclusion I is true
Only conclusion II is true
Either conclusion I or II is true
Neither conclusion I nor II is true
Both conclusions I and II are true

questions.explanation: Join the statements at R: P ≥ Q > R ≥ S = T. I: P to T has ≥, >, ≥, = with a strict sign: P > T. II: Q > R ≥ S = T gives Q > T, which is T < Q. Both are true.
solutionSteps: Join the statements at the shared letter R: P ≥ Q > R ≥ S = T.
I: one direction, one strict sign ⇒ P > T.
II: Q > R ≥ S = T ⇒ Q > T, i.e. T < Q.
questions.method: Merge the statements into one chain through the common letter.

hints.text: R appears in both statements; write one long chain through it.
II is written right to left: T < Q is the same as Q > T.

commonMistakes: Rejecting II because it is written in the opposite order.

questions.question: Which of the conclusions is definitely true?
questions.context:
Statements: A < B ≤ C; D ≥ C > E
Conclusions:
I. A < D
II. E < B

options.text: Only conclusion I is true
Only conclusion II is true
Either conclusion I or II is true
Neither conclusion I nor II is true
Both conclusions I and II are true

questions.explanation: Join at C: A < B ≤ C ≤ D (D ≥ C read the other way) and C > E. I: A < B ≤ C ≤ D gives A < D. II: from E to B: E < C ≥ B, opposite directions, so no relation. Only I.
solutionSteps: Rewrite D ≥ C > E around C: A < B ≤ C ≤ D, and C > E.
II: B ≤ C > E points both ways ⇒ no relation.
questions.method: Flip a statement carefully when you rewrite it the other way round.

hints.text: C is the shared letter.
Write D ≥ C as C ≤ D so the chain from A runs in one direction.

commonMistakes: Flipping the letters but not the sign when rewriting D ≥ C.

questions.question: Which of the conclusions is definitely true?
questions.context:
Statements: K = L ≥ M; N < M ≤ O
Conclusions:
I. K > N
II. O ≥ L

options.text: Only conclusion I is true
Only conclusion II is true
Either conclusion I or II is true
Neither conclusion I nor II is true
Both conclusions I and II are true

questions.explanation: Join at M: K = L ≥ M > N (N < M read the other way) and M ≤ O. I: K = L ≥ M > N gives K > N. II: from L to O: L ≥ M ≤ O, opposite directions, so no relation. Only I.
solutionSteps: Rewrite N < M as M > N: K = L ≥ M > N, and M ≤ O.
II: ≥ then ≤ ⇒ no relation between L and O.
questions.method: Merge through the common letter, then follow each path.

hints.text: M is the shared letter.
Between L and O the path goes down to M and back up.

commonMistakes: Concluding O ≥ L because both are "at least M".

questions.question: Which of the conclusions is definitely true?
questions.context:
Statements: F ≥ G = H; H > I ≤ J; J < K
Conclusions:
I. F > I
II. K > I

options.text: Only conclusion I is true
Only conclusion II is true
Either conclusion I or II is true
Neither conclusion I nor II is true
Both conclusions I and II are true

questions.explanation: Chain: F ≥ G = H > I ≤ J < K. I: F ≥ G = H > I gives F > I. II: from I to K: I ≤ J < K gives I < K, which is K > I. Both are true.
solutionSteps: Join the three statements at H and J: F ≥ G = H > I ≤ J < K.
II: ≤, < ⇒ I < K, i.e. K > I.
questions.method: Each conclusion only needs its own stretch of the chain.

hints.text: Two letters, H and J, link the three statements.
For II, start at I and walk towards K.

commonMistakes: Thinking the > before I spoils II: it is not on the path from I to K.

questions.question: Which of the conclusions is definitely true?
questions.context:
Statements: U > V ≥ W; X ≤ W < Y; Y = Z
Conclusions:
I. U > X
II. Z > V

options.text: Only conclusion I is true
Only conclusion II is true
Either conclusion I or II is true
Neither conclusion I nor II is true
Both conclusions I and II are true

questions.explanation: Join at W: U > V ≥ W ≥ X (X ≤ W read the other way) and W < Y = Z. I: U > V ≥ W ≥ X gives U > X. II: from Z to V: Z = Y > W ≤ V, opposite directions, so no relation. Only I.
solutionSteps: Rewrite around W: U > V ≥ W ≥ X, and W < Y = Z.
II: Z = Y > W, then W ≤ V: the path turns ⇒ no relation.
questions.method: Merge the chains at the shared letter; a path that goes down then up breaks.

hints.text: W is in the first two statements, Y in the last two.
Walk from Z to V: does the direction change at W?

commonMistakes: Accepting Z > V because both are bigger than W.

questions.question: Which of the conclusions is definitely true?
questions.context:

'P # Q' means 'P is neither smaller than nor equal to Q'.
'P $ Q' means 'P is neither smaller than nor greater than Q'.
'P % Q' means 'P is not greater than Q'.
'P & Q' means 'P is neither greater than nor equal to Q'.
Statements: P # Q; Q @ R; R $ S
Conclusions:
I. P # S
II. S & Q

options.text: Only conclusion I is true
Only conclusion II is true
Either conclusion I or II is true
Neither conclusion I nor II is true
Both conclusions I and II are true

questions.explanation: Decoded: # is >, @ is ≥, $ is =, & is <. The statements read P > Q ≥ R = S. I is P > S: true. II is S < Q, but Q ≥ R = S only gives Q ≥ S, so S < Q is not certain. Only I.
solutionSteps: Statements: P > Q ≥ R = S.
I: P > S true. II: S < Q not certain (only Q ≥ S).
questions.method: Decode every symbol before reading any conclusion.

hints.text: "Neither smaller than nor equal to" is >; "not smaller than" is ≥.
Decode the conclusions with the same key.

commonMistakes: Decoding @ (not smaller than) as >.

Conclusions:

options.text: Only conclusion I is true
Only conclusion II is true
Either conclusion I or II is true

questions.explanation: Decoded: A ≤ B < C ≥ D. I is A < C: from A ≤ B < C, true. II is D > A: the path D ≤ C > B ≥ A turns at C, so there is no definite relation. Only I.

I: ≤, < ⇒ A < C. II: path from A to D turns at C ⇒ no relation.

hints.text: "Not greater than" is ≤.
Between A and D, does the chain change direction?

Only conclusion II is true
Either conclusion I or II is true

M > O and M = O split M ≥ O ⇒ either I or II.

hints.text: Decode the statements and both conclusions.

questions.explanation: Decoded: H < J ≤ K = L. I is H < L: from H < J ≤ K = L, true. II is L ≥ J: from J ≤ K = L, J ≤ L, true. Both.

questions.question: Which sign should replace the question mark so that both conclusions are definitely true?
questions.context:
Expression: A < B ? C ≤ D
Conclusions that must definitely be true:
I. A < D
II. B < C
questions.explanation: II needs B < C exactly, so the sign must be <. Check I: A < B < C ≤ D gives A < D. With ≤ in its place, II would only give B ≤ C; with =, ≥ or > it fails.
solutionSteps: II involves only B and C, so the missing sign must say B < C.
Check I with < in place: A < B < C ≤ D ⇒ A < D.
questions.method: Use the conclusion that pins the missing sign down directly, then check the other.

hints.text: Conclusion II mentions only B and C, the letters either side of the "?".
Then check conclusion I with that sign in place.

commonMistakes: Choosing ≤, which gives only B ≤ C.

questions.question: Which sign should replace the question mark so that both conclusions are definitely true?
questions.context:
Expression: P = Q ? R ≤ S
Conclusions that must definitely be true:
I. P ≤ S
II. Q = R
questions.explanation: II needs Q = R, so the sign must be =. Check I: P = Q = R ≤ S gives P ≤ S. Any other sign breaks II.
solutionSteps: II is about Q and R, either side of "?": the sign must be =.
Check I: P = Q = R ≤ S ⇒ P ≤ S.
questions.method: An "=" conclusion needs "=" everywhere on its path.

hints.text: Look at II first: which letters does it link?
Q = R needs the sign between them to be "=".

commonMistakes: Choosing ≤ because the chain already has a ≤.

questions.question: Which sign should replace the question mark so that both conclusions are definitely true?
questions.context:
Expression: G ≥ H ? I ≥ J
Conclusions that must definitely be true:
I. G > J
II. H > I
questions.explanation: II needs H > I exactly, so the sign must be >. Check I: G ≥ H > I ≥ J gives G > J. With ≥, both conclusions would only be ≥.
solutionSteps: II links H and I, either side of "?": the sign must be >.
Check I: G ≥ H > I ≥ J ⇒ G > J (one strict sign).
questions.method: A strict conclusion needs at least one strict sign on its path.

hints.text: Which conclusion links exactly the two letters next to the "?"?
Is the path from G to J strict without the missing sign?

commonMistakes: Choosing ≥, which makes neither conclusion strict.

questions.question: Which of these conclusions are definitely true? Select all that apply.
questions.context: Statement: P ≥ Q > R = S ≤ T

options.text: P > R
T > R
S < P
Q = S

questions.explanation: P > R: P ≥ Q > R, true. T > R: T ≥ S = R gives only T ≥ R, not certain. S < P: P ≥ Q > R = S gives P > S, true. Q = S: Q > R = S gives Q > S, so Q = S is false.
solutionSteps: P to R: ≥, > ⇒ P > R.
R to T: =, ≤ ⇒ R ≤ T, so T > R is not certain.
P to S: ≥, >, = ⇒ P > S, i.e. S < P.
Q to S: >, = ⇒ Q > S, so Q = S is false.
questions.method: Check every option with the path rule.

hints.text: Follow the chain from the first letter of the conclusion to the second.
If a sign on that path points the other way (> against <, or ≥ against ≤), there is no definite relation.

commonMistakes: Selecting T > R: without a strict sign between R and T, only T ≥ R follows.

questions.question: Which pair of signs leaves no definite relation between X and Z?
questions.context: A chain reads X ? Y ? Z, with one sign between X and Y and another between Y and Z.

options.text: ≥ and >
= and <
> and ≤
≤ and <

questions.explanation: X > Y ≤ Z: X is above Y, and Z is at least Y, so Z could be above, equal to or below X. In the other pairs both signs point the same way (or one is =), so a relation always follows.
solutionSteps: ≥ and >: X ≥ Y > Z ⇒ X > Z.
= and <: X = Y < Z ⇒ X < Z.
> and ≤: the signs point opposite ways ⇒ no relation.
≤ and <: X ≤ Y < Z ⇒ X < Z.
questions.method: Opposite directions on a path mean no definite relation.

hints.text: Rewrite each pair as a chain X ? Y ? Z.
Which pair has one sign opening to the left and the other to the right?

commonMistakes: Choosing ≤ and <: two different signs, but they point the same way.
